name: Cipriano de Valera
title: Cipriano de Valera: revising a Bible for Spanish-speaking readers
description: The 1602 edition and the work of a Spanish reformer who wanted to put the Scriptures within reach of his readers.

sections.heading: A work received from other hands
paragraphs: Cipriano de Valera belonged to the world of the sixteenth-century Spanish Reformation. His life was connected with the monastery of San Isidoro del Campo in Seville and with Protestant exile. The story of his Bible work takes place outside Spain, at a time of intense religious conflict and restrictions on the circulation of books.

His name became linked with that of Casiodoro de Reina, whose translation of the Bible was published in 1569. Valera did not start a complete translation from scratch: he received an existing work and devoted his efforts to revising it. Distinguishing these tasks lets us recognize the service of both men without erasing their differences.

sections.heading: Reading, revising, and publishing again
paragraphs: In 1602 the second edition of that Bible, revised by Valera, appeared in Amsterdam. His exhortation to the reader explains his desire for the Spanish nation to have the Scriptures in its own language. He describes repeated readings, new notes, and changes in certain places in the text.

The image on the title page gave rise to the name Biblia del Cántaro (the “Pitcher Bible”). The later revisions known as Reina-Valera belong to a longer publishing history; not all of their decisions can be attributed to the 1602 edition. The exact date of Valera’s death remains uncertain.

reflection: First Corinthians 3:6–7 distinguishes between those who plant and those who water, and gives God the credit for the growth. That passage does not speak about any particular Bible edition, but it helps us think about shared work. Translating, revising, and making reading easier are tasks that require patience, knowledge, and humility.

Being grateful for a translation also means examining it carefully. We can learn from those who worked before us, recognize their limits, and help others understand what they read. Faithfulness to the Scriptures asks for more than admiring a name on the title page: it invites us to open the text and listen to it in context.
review_note: Translation and revision are distinguished. The uncertainty about his personal dates is kept; the date and place of publication follow the library catalog. The exhortation is summarized, not reproduced.
